title: CI/CD Is Dead, Agents Need Continuous Compute and Computers — Hugo Santos and Madison Faulkner

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's core subject is how coding agents and agentic software engineering break traditional CI/CD and require a new intent-and-plan-based development loop. The discussion centers on IDE and PR agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Amp, Factory) and the developer platform infrastructure supporting them. The talk addresses production CI/CD bottlenecks at agent scale and envisions scaling toward parallel multiverse development. Prerequisites include familiarity with CI/CD pipelines, GitHub Actions, PR workflows, and agent-based development tools. This is a conference presentation by two industry practitioners with slides and a chart demonstration. All evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct excerpts.

summary:
Madison Faulkner and Hugo Santos present a thesis that traditional CI/CD infrastructure is fundamentally mismatched with the emerging reality of agentic software development. CI/CD was designed for humans submitting one or two diffs per week, where human latency masked machine slowness. At agent scale—thousands of short-lived branches pulling the same codebase in different directions—systems hit runner saturation, cache thrash, and merge queues that behave like serialized database locks. GitHub commit activity has spiked dramatically in recent months, signaling this shift.

Their proposed replacement starts with acceleration: speeding up build, test, and deploy times by inserting an orchestration layer over existing GitHub Actions. The cache becomes the orchestration layer, requiring hardware-software co-design. The architecture includes intake with ingress shaping and rate limiting, cache orchestration routing to the right infrastructure, and agentic identity for software with retries at scale.

The new architecture removes PRs entirely. Development starts with intent and plan (a spec in a Linear ticket, Slack, or similar), fed into an agent loop harness (Claude Code, Amp, Cursor, Factory). The agent checks out a well-known commit, implements the plan, runs internal validation, and returns to the human for a continue/adjust decision. The harness adapts intent and plan as the codebase evolves, creating new loops. Completed changes enter a pre-merge queue for reconciliation, ensuring serializability before committing back to the repository ledger. Human review shifts from examining code diffs to reviewing intent-plus-outcome—potentially a video of the feature working or security LLM output—possibly across multiple semantically grouped changes. Namespace's own team sees 4x the PR volume of the past, making per-PR human review impossible.

Looking forward, they envision a multiverse where agents work on multiple commits simultaneously for the same plan, since the repository tip is a moving target. This requires an extremely fast inner loop and will cause resource usage to blow up. Efficiency comes from avoiding unnecessary work, not starting from scratch, and making agents work incrementally as engineers do on workstations. CI does not disappear but shifts: validation becomes continuous within the loop rather than a separate phase, coordination moves out of CI into the overall loop, and governance lifts into the harness that coerces changes to follow codified team processes. Compliance invariants like well-known checkouts are still enforced, but on a continuous basis.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and speaker bios
sections.summary: Madison Faulkner introduces herself as an NEA partner investing in infra and dev tools, formerly a Meta AI researcher. Hugo Santos is CEO of Namespace, building high-performance compute infrastructure, formerly led microservices at Google. They frame the talk around CI/CD being dead and continuous compute as its replacement.

sections.title: Why agentic software is breaking traditional CI/CD
sections.summary: The shift from monolithic agents to microservices with agents fragments the development lifecycle. Traditional CI/CD systems coexist with new IDEs and autonomous agentic engineering solutions. Human developers submit one or two diffs per week, masking machine slowness behind human latency.

sections.title: Problems with CI/CD at agent scale
sections.summary: At agent scale, thousands of short-lived branches pull the same codebase in different directions, making merging impossible. GitHub commit activity has spiked dramatically in recent months, with commit and lines-added-vs-deleted charts showing an unbelievable spike.

sections.title: Replacing CI/CD with acceleration and orchestration
sections.summary: The starting point for replacing CI/CD is acceleration—speeding up build, test, and deploy times by inserting over existing GitHub Actions. The cache becomes the orchestration layer via hardware-software co-design. Architecture includes intake with ingress shaping, cache orchestration, agentic identity, and retries at scale. Mitchell Hashimoto's proposed GitHub fixes are cited.

sections.title: Real-world solutions: human as agent and merge as database lock
sections.summary: Hugo describes working with Fall, Zed, Ramp, and others. Up to six months ago humans wrote all code slowly. Today code generation is cheap and continuous, forcing evaluation into the inner loop. The human is reframed as an agent cycling through PR review, test failures, and merge queue conflicts. Merging resembles high-performance database serialization with a single ledger requiring locks.

sections.title: New architecture: intent and plan-based development
sections.summary: The new architecture eliminates PRs entirely. Development starts with intent and plan—a spec in a Linear ticket, Slack, or elsewhere—fed into an agent loop harness (Claude Code, Amp, Cursor, Factory). The agent checks out a well-known commit, implements the plan, runs internal validation, returns to the human for a continue/adjust decision, then enters the merge queue. The Git repository functions as a ledger.

sections.title: Moving toward fully automated internal and external validation
sections.summary: Within weeks to months, code generation and inference will get faster. Internal validation must be extremely fast—15-45 minute runtimes are unacceptable. External validation will no longer have humans; specialized LLMs (security-focused, API conformance) will evaluate changes within the loop. Stateful environments with persistent memory are essential; cold starts introduce unacceptable delays.

sections.title: Pre-merge queue and human review of intent-plus-outcome
sections.summary: Completed changes don't go directly into the repository but enter a pre-merge queue for reconciliation, ensuring serializability when many parallel changes touch the same codebase. Human approval happens here, reviewing intent-plus-outcome rather than code—potentially a video of the feature working or security LLM output—possibly across multiple semantically grouped changes. Namespace's own team sees 4x the PR volume of the past, making per-PR human review impossible.

sections.title: The multiverse: parallel development across multiple commits
sections.summary: If the agent loop is extremely fast, development may step into a multiverse where agents work on multiple commits simultaneously for the same plan, since the repository tip is a moving target with many candidates. This causes resource usage to blow up. Efficiency strategies include avoiding unnecessary work, not starting from scratch, and having agents work incrementally as engineers do on workstations.

sections.title: Conclusion: CI shifts to continuous validation, governance lifts into harness
sections.summary: CI does not go away but shifts: validation becomes continuous within the loop rather than a separate phase. Coordination moves out of CI into the overall loop. Governance remains important but lifts into the harness, which coerces changes to follow codified team processes. Compliance invariants like well-known checkouts are still enforced, but on a continuous basis.
